title: Optimizing Electron Ptychography for Radiation-Sensitive Materials including Metal-Organic Frameworks
content: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is a widely employed technique for high-resolution imaging of nanomaterials. However, achieving atomic-resolution imaging of electron beam-sensitive materials—such as zeolites, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and organic-inorganic hybrid perovskites—remains a persistent challenge because of the low doses required to avoid radiation damage[1–4]. Recently, electron ptychography has gained attention as a promising solution to this issue, driven by advances in electron detector technologies that enable efficient acquisition of four-dimensional STEM (4D-STEM) datasets[5–7]. This technique offers several key advantages over conventional imaging methods: it is not limited by the traditional resolution constraints imposed by numerical apertures; it demonstrates remarkable tolerance to specimen thickness and provides depth resolution at the nanometer scale. Additionally, electron ptychography does not require a perfectly aberration-free probe and efficiently utilizes nearly all the signals in electron diffraction patterns to reconstruct phase images, enabling the simultaneous visualization of both heavy and light elements. These attributes make it particularly well-suited for low-dose imaging of beam-sensitive materials.
